blocks.text: On Sept. 19, 2001, Robert Stevens headed in to the offices of the Florida-based tabloid, Sun, where he worked as a photo editor. Waiting there was a letter: an unusual note, inside an envelope filled with a grainy white powder.

Mr. Stevens closely examined the letter before returning to work. It was, after all, unlike the publication’s usual mail: tabloid tips and notes from readers. But within days of opening that envelope, Mr. Stevens developed a deadly disease: inhalation anthrax.

He was the first of 22 people — primarily journalists, politicians and postal workers — to develop anthrax after handling powder-filled letters contaminated with a lab-grown strain of the bacteria, and the first of five people who died from the disease between October and November 2001.

The anthrax attacks further terrified a nation already on edge in the weeks after Sept. 11. Just as the Qaeda attacks had upended the country’s national security priorities, ushering in a sweeping electronic surveillance program and new rules for travelers at the airport, the anthrax attacks prompted a rethinking of the government’s approach to biosecurity.

Within weeks of Mr. Stevens’s death, new detection systems and response protocols were put in place around the country, and the federal response shifted from monitoring naturally occurring pathogens to seeking out man-made threats.

Now, 25 years later, experts warn that many of the systems put in place in 2001 have stagnated, leaving the country once again vulnerable. The technology meant to alert officials to a biological attack, experts say, is inefficient and outdated and the federal response remains largely uncoordinated and underfunded.
